figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: D-LSA design. Left: D-LSA (Flat). Indexer keys: 1 projection and L2 norm, 2 pooling (4:1), 3 bottom-up agglomerative clustering (Ward’s method), 4 bucket cache (centroids and index table). Indexer queries: A sum over query heads, projection and L2 norm, B scoring the cached centroids and selecting the top-p buckets per query, C expanding the buckets into indices (sink + top-k long-range + window), D attention over those indices (one index list per query shared by all query heads). Right: D-LSA (Tree) groups the buckets into a hierarchy of clusters, a query descends using beam search (close in the latent space but scattered through the KV cache).
figures.headline: D-LSA pools and clusters index keys into cached buckets, then each query selects top buckets and attends to their keys.
citing_sentences: We first describe this process, numbered as in Figure 3, which consists of semantic clustering of the index keys $k_{j}^{(\mathrm{idx})}$, and the search with the index queries $q_{i}^{(\mathrm{idx})}$ so that each query selects its keys.
Tree search arranges the buckets into a hierarchy (Figure 3, right).

D-LSA (Figure 3) follows the process outlined above, but since it distils from a pre-trained model which already has key and query projections ($k_{j}^{(\mathrm{attn})}$ and $q_{i}^{(\mathrm{attn})}$), we additionally learn separate key and query projections for LSA.

citing_sentences: N-LSA (Figure 4) trains LSA natively with the model, using only the NTP loss.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: N-LSA training speedup. Models trained natively on the NTP loss with Full Attention, SWA, NSA, PISA and N-LSA. Left: one attention layer, forward and backward, on one H200. Right: validation loss over the training time of the whole model in the decay phase (all on the same data and number of tokens).
figures.headline: N-LSA reaches full attention's validation loss of 1.085 at 128k tokens, while training 1.6× faster per layer.
citing_sentences: Figure 7 shows that N-LSA reaches the validation loss of Full Attention throughout the decay phase at 128k token context, at 1.085 against 1.085, while PISA, NSA and SWA trail at 1.100, 1.117 and 1.154.

For one attention layer on a single GPU, the forward and backward pass of N-LSA is 1.1$\times$ faster than Full Attention with FlashAttention-3 (Shah et al., 2024) at 64k tokens and 1.6$\times$ faster at 128k tokens (Figure 7, left).
End to end, the whole model completes its decay phase 1.24$\times$ faster at the same validation loss (Figure 7, right), as only every fourth layer is an attention layer.

citing_sentences: To test how many keys a query needs to keep accuracy, we let each query of Qwen-3.8-27B attend only to the sink, the window and its true top-$k$ keys (Figure 8).

figures.label: Figure 19
figures.caption: D-LSA with context parallelism (CP8). Top: prefill of GLM-5.3-Flash (PCP8 + DCP8), each rank holding a contiguous span of the query rows. Indexer keys: 1 projection of the whole chunk (on every rank), 2 bucket cache (the same on every rank). Indexer queries: A projection of the rank’s own rows, B selecting their index lists (other ranks’ rows lighter), C marking the selected prefix rows (a 1 B mask, merged across ranks), D gathering those rows from the ranks that hold them (padded), E attention of the rank’s own rows. Bottom: decode of GLM-5.3-Flash (PCP8 + DCP8) and Qwen-3.8-27B (TP8 + DCP8). Indexer keys: 1 projection of a complete cluster block (summed across ranks, once per block), 2 bucket cache. Indexer queries: A projection, B selecting the index list (the same on every rank), C attention over the entries the rank holds, D merging the partial outputs of the ranks (by log-sum-exp).

citing_sentences: CP splits work by token in two ways (Liu et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025a), which we describe in the following, and illustrate in Figure 19.
With MLA, we use both PCP and DCP (Figure 19, top), with no TP in the prefill attention, since SGLang was already developing PCP for GLM-5.3-Flash, while it had none for Qwen-3.8-27B.
In decode (Figure 19, bottom), each new token $j$ is written to its rank $r_{j}$, so the keys of a cluster block are spread across all ranks.

abstract: Agentic workflows are increasingly shifting towards long-horizon tasks, such as open-ended scientific work, where models benefit from long context windows. However, at ultra-long context (above 1M tokens), full attention is prohibitively expensive. A promising approach is sparse attention, in which a dedicated indexer selects a subset of keys for the attention. Yet current methods of indexing either still have quadratic cost in context size or lose accuracy at ultra-long context scale. We address this with Latent Sparse Attention (LSA), an efficient attention method that maintains accuracy at ultra-long context. In LSA, keys are hierarchically clustered in a learned latent space, and queries score the hierarchy of clusters instead of scoring every key, making prefill, decode and training faster at long context. We propose two variants, Distilled-LSA (D-LSA), which can be applied to pre-trained models via distillation, and Native-LSA (N-LSA), which is trained natively on the next-token loss alone. On GLM-5.3-Flash (Qwen-3.8-27B) at 10M tokens, D-LSA speeds up one attention layer by $22.7\times$ ($72.4\times$) in prefill and $4.6\times$ ($42.5\times$) in decode over its original sparse attention (full attention), while keeping similar accuracy across a variety of tasks. N-LSA matches the accuracy of full attention with a training speedup of $1.6\times$ per layer at 128k tokens. LSA offers practical and efficient attention for models to benefit from ultra-long context.

sections.body: The paper targets sparse attention above 1M tokens, where existing indexers still score every preceding key or block and can lose accuracy. It proposes Latent Sparse Attention (LSA), which clusters keys in a learned latent space and lets each query score the cluster hierarchy. Two variants are described: D-LSA, distilled into pre-trained models by training small projections per layer, and N-LSA, trained natively on the next-token loss alone. The contributions are evaluation on Qwen-3.8-27B and GLM-5.3-Flash up to 10M tokens on RULER and on a new benchmark, PaperTrail, integration into SGLang with GPU kernels for H200 and B300, and released code.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Sparse attention indexers that score every key dominate cost at ultra-long context, so LSA clusters keys instead.

sections.body: Full attention costs grow quadratically in prefill and linearly per decoded token. Sparse attention reduces the attention work to a fixed budget of k keys, but its indexer still scores all preceding keys. This remains quadratic in prefill and linear in decode, with smaller constant factors. In Figure 2, for one GLM-5.3-Flash global attention layer at 10M tokens, the indexer takes 98% of the prefill time of traditional sparse attention. A free indexer would make sparse attention a further 58× faster in prefill and 8.9× faster in decode. Existing cost reductions, such as block scoring and reusing selections across layers, divide the indexer cost by a constant.
sections.heading: Sparse Attention
sections.headline: At 10M tokens the indexer takes 98% of sparse attention's prefill time, and current indexers still scan every key.

sections.body: LSA pools consecutive index keys and clusters them bottom-up with Ward's method into buckets, keeping a bucket cache of centroids and index tables. Each query scores the bucket centroids, selects the top p buckets, and expands them into keys until k long-range keys are chosen. Attention then runs over sink keys, a window of the most recent cluster block, and those k keys. Flat search scores every centroid. Tree search groups buckets into levels and uses beam search, so a query scores O(log T) centroids. In D-LSA, index projections are learned by distilling the frozen model's attention with a KL loss. In N-LSA, the attention's own keys are clustered with a single key-value head and no added parameters.
sections.heading: Latent Sparse Attention (LSA)
sections.headline: LSA clusters keys in a learned latent space, and each query scores only bucket centroids, flat or as a tree.

sections.body: D-LSA is compared with full attention on Qwen-3.8-27B and with sparse attention on GLM-5.3-Flash, across knowledge, reasoning and long-context tasks. On GLM-5.3-Flash, D-LSA (Flat) uses k=2048 long-range keys before 1M tokens and k=4096 beyond. Figure 5 shows accuracy close to the baselines. One limit appears in the accuracy table: the D-LSA (Flat) row on Qwen-3.8-27B is -5.0 points on LongBench v2 relative to its baseline. N-LSA is a hybrid model of about 0.5B parameters, trained on 100B tokens of FineWeb-Edu and then 12B tokens of LongDocs at 128k tokens. Its validation loss is 1.085 against 1.085 for full attention, while PISA, NSA and SWA reach 1.100, 1.117 and 1.154. On RULER at 128k tokens, N-LSA scores 32.2 against 34.7 for full attention.
sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.headline: D-LSA keeps accuracy close to baselines up to 10M tokens, and N-LSA matches full-attention validation loss at 128k.

sections.body: The section lists limits. LSA reduces the cost of finding keys but not of storing them, because the KV cache still grows linearly with context. Tree search loses accuracy faster than flat search past 1M tokens on GLM-5.3-Flash. It overtakes flat search in decode only from about 5M tokens with one request, and is predicted to do so in prefill only beyond 10M tokens. It remains open whether sparse training would close this gap beyond indexer distillation. N-LSA was trained at about 0.5B parameters, up to 128k tokens, with flat search only. Scaling native training to larger models, longer contexts and tree search is left open.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: Tree search loses accuracy faster than flat past 1M tokens, and native training was tested only at small scale.

sections.body: LSA addresses the cost of finding keys in sparse attention at ultra-long context. D-LSA distils LSA into pre-trained models and stays close to baseline accuracy up to 10M tokens. At 10M tokens, one attention layer prefills 22.7× and decodes 4.6× faster than sparse attention in GLM-5.3-Flash. It prefills 72.4× and decodes 42.5× faster than Full Attention in Qwen-3.8-27B. End to end, time to first token is reduced by 2.2× and 9.2×, respectively. N-LSA trains natively on the next-token loss alone, at the accuracy of Full Attention and 1.6× faster per layer at 128k tokens. The authors describe LSA as a practical way forward for ultra-long context attention.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: LSA offers a practical route to ultra-long context attention, through distillation of pre-trained models or native training.

sections.body: Appendix A tests how many keys a query needs. At 128k tokens, Top-k Oracle Attention keeps 98% of the RULER accuracy of Full Attention down to k=512, while each query attends to 0.8% of the keys. Further sections give the symbols of LSA, the clustering and beam search algorithms, and the LongDocs training data, including 352M distillation tokens. They also cover the construction of PaperTrail with its 1,246 papers, tiers and controls, the evaluation setup, per-task RULER results, reasoning token counts, the block size comparison, and the kernel and parallelism details.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers oracle key-budget tests, method symbols, training data, PaperTrail, evaluation setup, and parallelism details.
